text:
American Federation of Teachers (AFT) President Randi Weingarten promoted a nationwide back-to-school boycott of retail giant Target over the weekend because the company had not condemned ICE operations in Minnesota — the location of its headquarters — prompting criticism from education advocates and a call for federal scrutiny.

"We gave Target ample time to stand with the communities in which they operate and help their neighbors, but its silence about federal immigration abuses has been deafening," Weingarten said in a statement.

"The issue could not be more pressing: Seven months since the murders of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, masked ICE agents are still in our streets, our schools and our communities, terrorizing families in the name of Donald Trump’s illegal and immoral assault on immigrants striving for their American Dream," she continued. "That’s why we’re urging our members to avoid Target and patronize more ethical shopping alternatives this back-to-school season."

Weingarten also shared a video on Instagram, where she directed families to the AFT’s "Shop Smart, Not Target" website, which maps local back-to-school shopping alternatives. The organization launched the campaign Wednesday after sending Target CEO Michael Fiddelke letters in February and March.

WATCH: WEINGARTEN GESTURES WILDLY DURING ANTI-TRUMP RANT, LATER SAYS HE DRIVES HER TO DRINK

In a statement to Fox News Digital, DHS rejected the AFT's characterization of ICE.

"ICE enforces federal immigration laws, protects public safety, and conducts enforcement pursuant to federal laws and applicable agency policies. Target is not a sensitive location," an ICE spokesperson said. "However, the current policy provides guidance for officers and recognizes that enforcement actions in or near protected areas require consideration of the circumstances and applicable law. ICE will continue to conduct lawful actions wherever necessary to protect the American people."

The spokesperson further said that ICE did not target schools and called AFT's statement a false narrative.

"This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement, who are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson said.

"ICE is not going to schools to arrest children—we are protecting children. Criminals are no longer able to hide in America’s schools to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement and instead trusts them to use common sense. If a dangerous illegal alien felon were to flee into a school, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect public safety," they said.

"ICE’s position remains straightforward: its officers enforce the immigration laws enacted by Congress and carry out the agency’s mission to protect national security and public safety. ICE is engaged in targeted law enforcement operations to apprehend and remove aliens in the country unlawfully and will continue to do so despite grandstanding by politicians and criminal illegal alien supporters," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Aliens placed into removal proceedings receive due process. Once it is exhausted, ICE carries out the removal order. Dangerous rhetoric from politicians and activists demonizing our brave ICE officers has led to the over 8,000% increase in threats against DHS law enforcement who are heroically performing their congressionally mandated mission to remove criminal illegal aliens from communities across the country."

TEACHERS UNION FACING YEARS OF DEFICITS SEEKS TO BECOME OREGON'S LARGEST PAC, INTERNAL DOCUMENTS SHOW

Corey DeAngelis, a Heritage Foundation research fellow, told Fox News Digital Sunday that using the organization’s pension influence against Target raised fiduciary concerns and warranted a federal investigation.

"This partisan war on Target smells like a breach of fiduciary duty given that AFT members’ pension funds own 6.79 million shares of Target stock, which Weingarten has already leveraged to pressure the company into opposing ICE," he said. "The Department of Justice should open an investigation into the AFT using their pension funds and political influence to bully companies into falling in line with their socialist agenda."

"Urging educators and families to avoid Target is not an appropriate use of the union’s resources or influence," he added.

This isn't the AFT's first time batting against the retail giant.

DeAngelis also supplied Fox News Digital with a chart tracking Target’s closing share price against several AFT actions, including Weingarten’s letters and the organization’s March boycott resolution.

Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction and Chino Valley Unified School District board president, told Fox News Digital on Sunday that labor leaders were prioritizing political power while students continued to struggle academically.

"Teachers’ unions are supposed to fight for teachers. Instead, union leadership has become a political machine obsessed with money, power and influence while our children continue to fall behind," she said. "In California, more than half our students are not proficient in basic reading and math. When a system produces those results year after year, that isn’t success. That’s education malpractice."

California's latest statewide assessments showed 48.8% of students met or exceeded English language arts standards and 37.3% met or exceeded math standards.

The AFT's March resolution explicitly called the effort a boycott and urged its 1.8 million members, families and allies to avoid Target until the company stood with the Twin Cities.

TEXAS’ LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT SEES TEST SCORES SOAR AFTER STATE TAKEOVER DESPITE RACISM CLAIMS

DeAngelis’ request followed the July appeal by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., for the Labor Department to investigate whether AFT leaders coordinated with retirement-plan fiduciaries to use members’ assets for political objectives.

House lawmakers separately demanded answers about reports that member dues helped finance Weingarten’s book, "Why Fascists Fear Teachers," while she received royalties.

Teachers spend an average of $895 of their own money every year on supplies their students need, according to a 2025 teacher spending survey.

title: UNO grad's aim to soar as U.S. pilot dashed by immigration status, despite Rep. Bacon's intervention
description:

But her plan has been thwarted by immigration legal problems.
When she was a teen, unbeknownst to her until later, an immigration judge had ordered her removed from the country.

text:
OMAHA — Ever since she can remember, Mariana Juarez wanted to fly.

A commercial pilot’s license seemed a distant dream, though, when family hardships in her home in Guerrero, Mexico, drove her out of school at age 14.

Two years later, she and her mom fled to the United States without authorization. They were allowed to stay while the federal government weighed their cases. But shortly afterward, Juarez said, depression gripped her mom and she returned to Mexico, leaving her daughter with relatives in Omaha.

With the help of a cousin, Juarez enrolled in high school, won a full-ride private scholarship and this year graduated from the University of Nebraska at Omaha with honors and an aviation degree. Along the way she worked full time, obtained a private pilot’s license and, at age 24, was in the process of achieving certification as a commercial pilot.

But her plan has been thwarted by immigration legal problems. When she was a teen, unbeknownst to her until later, an immigration judge had ordered her removed from the country.

Despite the weight of a well-known legal team — and intervention from a Republican congressman — Homeland Security officials have declined to reverse course and allow her to stay legally.

Juarez plans a September return to the homeland she hasn’t seen in eight years. She chose to buy a one-way ticket out rather than risk detention amid President Donald Trump’s mass deportation push, which he argues protects U.S. jobs, public resources and public safety.

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska’s Omaha-heavy 2nd District said he met Juarez and went to the top seeking a different outcome, twice speaking to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He said he was told — most recently this past week — there’d be no exception.

“It’s an unchristian policy we’re seeing here,” Bacon said in an interview with the Examiner. “I get it, we wanted to secure the borders. I think we’ve done that. We don’t want dangerous people here, I get it. But what’s going on here is a terrible overreach, a terrible injustice.”

Bacon, a retired Air Force brigadier general wrapping up his fifth term, said he’s armed with examples of other constituents, and is calling on Republican colleagues to support immigration reform that “makes sense.”

Teen steered her own path in foreign land

Juarez launched her U.S. education in 2018, in the halls of the largest high school in Nebraska’s most populated city.

By the time she enrolled in Martha Omar’s senior English class at Omaha Central High, the teen had learned a second language and had become a “bridge” helping other immigrant students adjust.

“She was a student that struck me as someone navigating high school by herself,” said Omar, a teacher of 20 years. “She was getting herself to school and home on her own, and was always working a job during high school.”

Omar said Juarez impressed her to the point that after her 2022 graduation, she hired her former student to tutor her two sons in Spanish. Years later, Juarez remains a close family friend, picking the boys up sometimes for adventures such as Sky Zone. Omar called the predicament heartbreaking.

“As a teacher we pour into our students and our dream is they go on to thrive in our community,” she said. “When you have kids like Mariana that have this incredible talent and bravery and drive … what’s better to have in a community than that?”

While at Central, Juarez knew she wanted to go to college, the first in her family to do so, and dived into research.

What she didn’t know until it was too late, said her attorney Roxana Cortes-Mills, was that in the fall of 2018 an immigration court had sent notice of a hearing to a residence she had shared with her mom.

Cortes-Mills said she found the notice in Juarez’s official immigration file marked as undeliverable and “return to sender.”

Juarez did not show up at the hearing, and an Omaha immigration judge on Oct. 24, 2018, ordered her removed from the country.

“She was 17 years old,” a minor under Nebraska and federal law, said Cortes-Mills, legal director for the Center for Immigrant and Refugee Advancement. “That hearing happened. She didn’t attend. She didn’t know.”

No lawful status, no pilot’s license

As Mariana explored her dream career, she said she learned she could not obtain a U.S. pilot’s license without a lawful status.

In 2022, she sought assistance from CIRA (formerly known as Immigrant Legal Center) and the nonprofit’s legal experts explained consequences of the removal order. They said she was beyond eligibility for special immigrant juvenile status for minors deemed by a court to have been abused or abandoned by a parent.

A subsequent effort to reopen Juarez’s case due to not receiving the hearing notice was denied April 24, 2024, according to Board of Immigration Appeals records. Cortes-Mills said the legal team did not pursue a further challenge based upon a new high court ruling that at the time seemed to rule out a chance.

That year, federal officials did offer a form of relief to Juarez — a temporary stay of removal, which she said allowed her to obtain work authorization while in college and cleared the way for a private pilot license in 2025. She said a private license is a step toward her commercial license.

This summer, however, immigration officials denied Juarez another extension for a third year on the stay of removal.

Homeland Security officials, in response to a request for comment, offered a three-paragraph statement that pointed to the immigration court’s 2018 removal order. A spokesperson’s email said Juarez and her mother had applied for admission through the San Ysidro Port of Entry and that neither had legal documents to enter the U.S.

The department, which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement, in January claimed “an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations and more than 675,000 deportations” in the first year since Trump returned as president in 2025. Homeland Security said the crackdown set the stage to break more records and save taxpayer dollars.

Juarez — faced with a U.S. future without a work permit, driver’s license and risk of detention — said her $400 Mexico-bound ticket is set for early September.

Tearing up, the UNO grad who had started working at CIRA greeting clients, said leaving is not her preference but that she knew each renewal of a stay of removal was uncertain. She said she appreciates the friends she’s made and her U.S. education.

Her UNO degree reflects a concentration in air transport administration, and she hopes while in Mexico to validate her training thus far and resume her quest to be a professional commercial pilot.

Juarez, whose roots are in the southwest Mexican state of Guerrero, recalls visiting an airport as a child and seeing the joy on people’s faces as a plane connected them to family or adventure.

“Since I was a kid, I didn’t see myself being anything else,” she said. “I wanted to be in the sky.”

Sitting in university aviation classes dominated by males strengthened her resolve. Juarez said she became more motivated.

One “extreme” to the next?

Bacon — who has been in the national spotlight as one of a small number of Republicans in Congress critical of the president, but who also said he has learned to pick his battles — said he sees “no goodness” in ousting Juarez. Bacon said his staff worked many hours on her case.

He cited a recent Gallup poll, which showed that 73% of Americans believe immigration is a “good thing” for the country. That share slipped from a record high of 79% last year, but remains above the 25-year trend average of 67%, the pollster in July said of its June telephone survey.

Bacon said the “real issue” is an outdated system of immigration laws and policies. He said “we went from one extreme” under Joe Biden to “another extreme” under Donald Trump.

Bacon believes the current extreme will hurt his party in the midterms.

A backer of the stalled Dignity Act of 2025, Bacon wants Congress to create a path for contributing and working migrants to legally stay. That bipartisan bill, championed by Rep. Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, and Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat, drew support from across party lines and multiple states, offering border protections, asylum and immigration reforms but no amnesty or citizenship to those who entered illegally.

“We can put a little common sense and humanity into the equation,” Bacon said.

Bryan Slone, former chief executive of the statewide Nebraska Chamber of Commerce & Industry who currently is a pilot trainee, continues to work on workforce issues and touts an overhaul of the immigration system as a way to help the state’s labor shortage.

A registered nonpartisan, Slone considers talented yet undocumented migrants schooled in Nebraska a smart recruitment and retention pool, and he urges bipartisan solutions.

“We still have the ‘brain drain’ issue and we still have the declining birth rate issue that we’ve been talking about for four or five years,” he said.

Ariel Ruiz Soto, senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C., nonpartisan think-tank, said part of the conversation often missing is what happens to migrants after they return or are removed to their homeland.

He said brain drain, or exodus of young educated talent, can be viewed as “brain gain” for the other side.

Ruiz Soto said the Mexican government, for example, has tried to “make the most of this brain gain.” Among reintegration resources it offers is the “Mexico te abraza” (Mexico embraces you) program. Returning or deported nationals at various reentry points can access support ranging from food to employment assistance.

Juarez said she hopes her journey will inspire young immigrants with U.S. voting power to speak out on issues facing their community.

With her eye on a flight program in Mexico, she said she will “keep chasing my dreams,” albeit in a country other than the U.S.

title: Cuban and Other Trump Deportees Sent to 'Do Not Travel' African Nation Say: 'We Cannot Leave'
description:
Dozens of foreign nationals deported from the United States have found themselves stranded in the conflict-ridden Central African Republic under expanding third-country deportation agreements.
The controversial practice of sending deportees to unstable third countries has intensified legal and humanitarian scrutiny surrounding modern immigration enforcement.
Deportees living in temporary housing in Bangui explain that they have no practical way to leave the country.
Separation From Families and Children The human cost of these third-country removals is deeply felt by families remaining in the United States.
Do you believe the United States should be allowed to deport individuals to third countries if returning them to their home nation poses a threat to their safety?
text:
Dozens of foreign nationals deported from the United States have found themselves stranded in the conflict-ridden Central African Republic under expanding third-country deportation agreements.

Men from nations including Cuba, Eritrea, Ecuador, Honduras, Serbia, Russia, and Vietnam report arriving in the impoverished African nation with no prior notice, no local ties, and no identification documents. Many of these individuals had lived in the United States for years, establishing families and securing legal protections against deportation to their home countries due to fears of torture or persecution.

Now trapped in the capital city of Bangui, the deportees describe navigating severe economic hardship, language barriers, and profound separation from their loved ones.

The controversial practice of sending deportees to unstable third countries has intensified legal and humanitarian scrutiny surrounding modern immigration enforcement.

A Sudden Arrival in an Unfamiliar Land

Immigrants transported across the globe express shock and confusion after being relocated to one of the most volatile regions in the world.

For Cuban national Yasmany Moreno de Armas, the journey began after living and working in Florida for nearly a decade. Following an arrest by immigration authorities over expired parole status, the 31-year-old spent approximately a year in federal custody before discovering he had been flown directly to the Central African Republic.

The landlocked nation currently faces severe armed conflict and political instability, prompting the U.S. State Department to maintain a Level 4 travel advisory urging Americans not to visit.

Deportees living in temporary housing in Bangui explain that they have no practical way to leave the country. Moreno de Armas shared that he had never even heard of the nation prior to his arrival and now struggles with having no identification papers or financial resources.

The abrupt relocation has left many feeling effectively stateless in an environment where they cannot speak the local language or contact legal representation easily.

Separation From Families and Children

The human cost of these third-country removals is deeply felt by families remaining in the United States.

Eritrean native Zena Gebrgzabher was also among those sent to the African nation after years of building a stable life in Maryland. Working as a commercial truck driver, Gebrgzabher lived alongside his wife and their five-year-old son, both of whom are American citizens.

His sudden removal occurred during a routine check-in with immigration officials, leaving his young family devastated and struggling to explain his absence to their child.

His wife described the deportation as profoundly unfair, noting that their young son constantly asks when his father will return home. Because Gebrgzabher has no personal connections or relatives in the region, his family remains deeply concerned for his physical safety.

The emotional strain is compounded by the fact that neither man had a serious criminal record beyond immigration and minor traffic violations.

Legal Loopholes and Third-Country Pacts

The deportations highlight how bilateral agreements allow authorities to circumvent standard deportation barriers.

Under federal immigration policy, the government has established agreements with more than thirty nations to accept foreign deportees. These third-country pacts are frequently utilized when an immigrant's home nation limits or refuses repatriation flights, or when an individual has won specific protections in immigration court.

In Gebrgzabher's case, an immigration judge granted him protection under the Convention Against Torture in 2017, which legally barred authorities from returning him to Eritrea due to past military conscription and detention. However, that ruling did not grant formal permanent asylum, leaving a legal opening for officials to remove him to a third nation instead.

Similarly, Moreno de Armas faced documented risks of persecution in Cuba for previously attempting to flee the island, making third-country transfer a mechanism to execute removal orders despite local dangers.

Humanitarian Concerns and Legal Precedents

Advocates and affected individuals argue that transferring immigrants to third countries creates unacceptable safety and ethical risks.

Immigration attorneys and human rights observers warn that sending individuals to nations experiencing civil strife exposes them to severe physical dangers. The lack of consular representation, local integration programs, or basic travel documentation leaves deportees highly vulnerable to exploitation and violence in unfamiliar environments.

Both Moreno de Armas and Gebrgzabher emphasized that deportation policies should focus on returning individuals to their homelands rather than displacing them into foreign cultures.

As additional countries enter third-country agreements, legal challenges are expected to test whether sending protected individuals to conflict zones complies with international humanitarian standards.

Question for you. Do you believe the United States should be allowed to deport individuals to third countries if returning them to their home nation poses a threat to their safety?

title: Why did a US judge strike down Trump's immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries
description:
The lawsuit was brought by immigrant rights organisations, immigrant visa applicants and U.S. citizens seeking to sponsor family members abroad.
Judge Jeannette Vargas concluded that the State Department’s immigrant visa suspension conflicted directly with the structure established by federal immigration law.
The State Department justified the suspension primarily through concerns that immigrant visa applicants from the affected countries were more likely to become a “public charge” after entering the United States.
The suspension applied to immigrant visa applicants from 75 countries spanning several regions, making it one of the administration’s most geographically extensive restrictions on legal immigration.
The judgment significantly limits the administration’s ability to use the public-charge concept as the basis for a nationality-wide immigrant visa suspension.
text:
A federal judge in New York has struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance for applicants from 75 countries, ruling that the State Department exceeded the authority granted to it under federal immigration law.

Judge Jeannette Vargas of the Southern District of New York described the policy as “patently unlawful,” finding that Secretary of State Marco Rubio could not categorically prevent consular officers from adjudicating immigrant visa applications solely because of an applicant’s nationality.

The decision concerns a policy that took effect in January and affected applicants across Latin America, the Balkans, South Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean. Countries covered by the suspension included Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Bosnia, Albania, Pakistan and Bangladesh. The State Department had defended the measure by arguing that applicants from the designated countries faced a heightened risk of becoming a “public charge,” meaning they could potentially rely on government resources after entering the United States.

The lawsuit was brought by immigrant rights organisations, immigrant visa applicants and U.S. citizens seeking to sponsor family members abroad. Their central argument was that the administration had effectively created a nationality-based bar that Congress had not authorised.

The ruling is significant because it does not simply challenge the administration’s immigration policy on political or humanitarian grounds. It focuses on the legal limits of executive authority and the division of power between Congress and the executive branch. The administration may retain substantial authority over immigration and national security, but the court held that this authority does not permit the State Department to rewrite the statutory rules governing immigrant visa eligibility.

The case therefore has implications beyond the immediate 75-country suspension. It raises broader questions about how far a president or cabinet secretary can go in restricting immigration through executive action, how nationality can legally be used in visa decisions and whether other recent immigration restrictions could face similar judicial scrutiny.

What exactly did Judge Jeannette Vargas rule?

Judge Jeannette Vargas concluded that the State Department’s immigrant visa suspension conflicted directly with the structure established by federal immigration law. Her ruling focused on the principle that consular officers are required to adjudicate visa applications according to statutory eligibility criteria rather than automatically rejecting or refusing to process them because an applicant holds the nationality of a designated country.

The judge wrote that the policy “categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant” and therefore represented a direct departure from the statutory framework enacted by Congress.

That distinction is legally important. The executive branch has broad authority over foreign relations, border policy and immigration enforcement, but those powers are not unlimited when Congress has created a detailed legal regime governing who may receive an immigrant visa and how applications must be assessed.

The court’s reasoning suggests that the State Department cannot substitute a blanket administrative rule for individual adjudication when the law requires applications to be considered under specified criteria. In other words, an applicant may still be denied an immigrant visa for legally recognised reasons, including admissibility grounds or public-charge considerations, but the government cannot simply declare that applicants from an entire nationality group are ineligible without a statutory basis.

The ruling therefore targets the mechanism of the policy rather than declaring that the administration has no authority to regulate immigration. The problem, according to the court, was that the State Department effectively created a new nationality-based exclusion category without Congress authorising it.

That is why the decision may have broader consequences. If other immigration restrictions similarly rely on executive interpretation rather than explicit statutory authority, courts may examine whether the administration is enforcing existing law or attempting to create new legal barriers through policy directives.

The administration could challenge the ruling on appeal, potentially arguing that the executive branch possesses greater authority in visa and national security matters than the district court recognised. For now, however, Vargas’s decision represents a clear judicial rejection of this particular policy.

Why did the Trump administration impose the 75-country visa suspension?

The State Department justified the suspension primarily through concerns that immigrant visa applicants from the affected countries were more likely to become a “public charge” after entering the United States. The public-charge concept has long existed in U.S. immigration law and allows authorities, under certain circumstances, to consider whether an applicant is likely to become primarily dependent on government assistance.

The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to interpret immigration law in ways that place greater emphasis on financial self-sufficiency. In this case, the State Department appears to have concluded that applicants from certain countries presented a sufficiently elevated risk that immigrant visa issuance should be suspended more broadly.

The policy therefore fit within the administration’s wider immigration strategy, which has combined national security arguments, economic self-sufficiency requirements and tighter scrutiny of legal immigration channels.

However, the court found that the administration went beyond applying the public-charge standard to individual applicants. Instead, the policy used nationality as a categorical basis for suspending visa issuance across 75 countries.

That was the central legal vulnerability. Public-charge determinations are generally based on an individual applicant’s circumstances, including factors that may relate to finances, sponsorship and likely dependence on public assistance. A nationality-wide prohibition replaces that individual analysis with a presumption applying to an entire country or group of countries.

The administration may argue that statistical or policy-based risk assessments are necessary to manage migration efficiently and protect public resources. Governments routinely use broader categories in screening, security and foreign policy.

But the court’s ruling indicates that such policy judgments must still operate within the boundaries Congress established. If federal law does not permit immigrant visas to be withheld solely on nationality grounds in the manner used here, the State Department cannot create that authority administratively.

The decision therefore exposes a recurring tension in U.S. immigration policy: the executive branch often seeks rapid, broad measures to achieve policy objectives, while courts examine whether those measures remain within the legal powers delegated by Congress.

Which applicants and countries were affected by the policy?

The suspension applied to immigrant visa applicants from 75 countries spanning several regions, making it one of the administration’s most geographically extensive restrictions on legal immigration.

The affected states included countries in Latin America, the Balkans, South Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean. Among those specifically identified were Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Bosnia, Albania, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

The impact was particularly significant because immigrant visas are generally intended for people seeking permanent residence in the United States rather than short-term travel. The policy therefore affected individuals attempting to relocate permanently, often through family-based or other established immigration channels.

Many applicants had U.S.-based sponsors, including American citizens petitioning for relatives. This meant the consequences were not limited to foreign nationals abroad. U.S. citizens and lawful residents could also experience prolonged family separation because their relatives’ applications were effectively blocked.

That domestic connection became important in the lawsuit. The plaintiffs included not only immigrant rights groups and visa applicants but also U.S. citizens sponsoring family members. Their involvement strengthened the argument that the policy had direct consequences for people already living legally in the United States.

The geographic breadth of the suspension also contributed to accusations that it was overly sweeping. Treating applicants from dozens of countries as presumptively problematic based on broad public-charge concerns raised questions about whether nationality was being used as a substitute for individual assessment.

For applicants, the practical consequences could include delayed reunification, postponed relocation plans, financial uncertainty and the expiration of documents or administrative approvals obtained earlier in the immigration process.

Even after the court’s ruling, immediate resolution for every affected applicant is not guaranteed. Administrative implementation, possible appeals and the individual circumstances of pending cases could determine how quickly visa processing resumes.

Nevertheless, the judgment removes, at least at the district court level, the legal basis for using the 75-country suspension as a blanket prohibition.

Why is the ruling a setback for Trump’s broader immigration agenda?

The decision is significant because the visa suspension was not an isolated policy. It formed part of a broader series of immigration restrictions introduced after Donald Trump returned to office.

The administration has pursued a more restrictive approach across multiple parts of the immigration system, including entry restrictions, immigrant visa processing and diversity visa programmes. Rights groups have challenged several of these measures, arguing that the administration is using executive authority to impose limitations that Congress did not clearly authorise.

The ruling therefore matters strategically. A court decision invalidating one major policy can provide legal arguments for challenging related measures if they rely on similar reasoning or administrative mechanisms.

At the same time, the ruling does not automatically invalidate every other Trump immigration restriction. Different policies may rely on different statutory authorities, national security powers or presidential proclamations. Courts will assess each measure according to its own legal basis.

This distinction is important because presidents traditionally receive substantial judicial deference in immigration and foreign affairs, particularly when national security is invoked. Previous litigation over travel restrictions has demonstrated that executive authority can be extensive when Congress has delegated specific powers.

The problem for the administration in this case was that the court found Secretary Rubio’s action incompatible with the existing statutory scheme.

That creates a potentially important boundary. The administration may be able to impose strict eligibility standards, increase vetting or use authorities explicitly granted by Congress, but it cannot necessarily achieve the same result through categorical nationality-based suspensions if federal law requires individual adjudication.

Politically, the ruling also gives immigration advocacy groups momentum. Successful challenges can encourage additional litigation and increase scrutiny of executive policies introduced through departmental directives rather than legislation.

For the White House, the decision may reinforce the importance of choosing legal authorities carefully. Broad immigration restrictions can be politically attractive because they can be implemented rapidly, but they are also more vulnerable if courts conclude that the executive branch has exceeded its statutory mandate.

How does this case differ from broader US travel bans?

The 75-country immigrant visa suspension should be distinguished from broader travel bans because the legal mechanisms and categories of people affected can differ substantially.

A travel ban may restrict entry into the United States under presidential authority that Congress has expressly delegated for situations in which the president determines that the entry of certain foreign nationals would be detrimental to U.S. interests.

An immigrant visa suspension administered by the State Department operates differently. It concerns whether consular officers may issue visas under the statutory immigration framework. The court in this case focused on whether the secretary of state had authority to stop issuance based categorically on nationality.

That distinction can produce very different legal outcomes even when two policies appear similar in practical effect.

The Center for Constitutional Rights noted that the immigrant visa freeze followed other restrictive measures, including a broader travel ban covering 39 countries that took effect on January 1 and a pause on diversity visa issuance in late December.

Those measures may be challenged separately, but Vargas’s ruling does not automatically determine their legality. A court examining another policy would need to identify the specific statutory authority invoked, the procedural basis for the restriction and whether the executive branch acted within the discretion Congress granted.

This is one reason immigration litigation can appear inconsistent to the public. Courts may uphold one nationality-based restriction while striking down another because the underlying legal authorities differ.

The administration is likely to emphasise national security and executive discretion when defending such measures. Rights groups, by contrast, tend to focus on statutory limits, due process and discriminatory effects.

The current ruling strengthens the argument that nationality alone cannot be used freely across every part of immigration law. But it does not establish a universal prohibition against nationality-based distinctions.

The broader legal battle will therefore revolve around the precise source of executive authority in each case and whether Congress has clearly permitted the government to impose the restriction at issue.

What does the ruling mean for the public-charge argument?

The judgment significantly limits the administration’s ability to use the public-charge concept as the basis for a nationality-wide immigrant visa suspension.

Public-charge rules are designed to evaluate whether an individual applicant is likely to become dependent on public resources. Historically, that assessment involves facts specific to the person rather than a categorical determination based solely on citizenship.

The State Department attempted to justify the 75-country suspension by arguing that applicants from those countries presented a heightened public-charge risk.

The judge’s decision indicates that even if the government possesses data suggesting differences in economic outcomes among immigrant groups, that does not necessarily permit it to suspend visa issuance for entire nationalities.

This is important because it preserves the distinction between risk assessment and legal eligibility.

An immigration officer may be authorised to examine income, sponsorship, financial resources or other relevant factors. But replacing those individual inquiries with a nationality-based presumption may conflict with statutory requirements.

The ruling therefore does not eliminate the public-charge doctrine. The administration may continue applying lawful public-charge standards to individual applicants, provided those standards comply with federal law and applicable regulations.

What the court rejected was the use of public-charge concerns as a justification for an across-the-board nationality ban.

This distinction could influence future policy design. If the administration wants to tighten public-charge screening, it may need to revise individual eligibility criteria rather than impose geographic or nationality-based suspensions.

That approach would likely be more administratively complex because consular officers would have to evaluate each applicant separately. But it would also align more closely with the legal framework described by the court.

For immigrant rights groups, the decision reinforces the argument that poverty or nationality cannot be transformed into automatic disqualifying categories without congressional approval.

For the administration, the challenge is balancing its goal of limiting dependence on public resources with legal requirements mandating individual adjudication.

The dispute therefore extends beyond one visa freeze and touches on a fundamental policy question: how much discretion should immigration officials have to translate demographic or economic risk assessments into categorical restrictions?

Could the Trump administration appeal the decision?

The administration can seek appellate review, and an appeal would be a predictable next step if the Justice Department and State Department conclude that the ruling improperly restricts executive authority.

An appeal would likely focus on several legal questions. The government could argue that the secretary of state has broader discretion over visa issuance than the district court recognised, particularly when implementing immigration policy connected to national interests.

It could also challenge the court’s interpretation of the statutory framework and contend that the policy was a permissible administrative response to public-charge concerns rather than an unlawful creation of a new nationality-based exclusion.

If the administration appeals, it may also seek a stay that would temporarily prevent the district court’s decision from taking full effect while litigation continues. Whether such relief is granted would depend on the appellate court’s assessment of factors including the government’s likelihood of success and potential harm to both sides.

The litigation could therefore continue for months or potentially longer.

If appellate courts ultimately agree with Judge Vargas, the ruling could establish a stronger precedent limiting the State Department’s ability to impose similar nationality-based immigrant visa restrictions.

If the administration succeeds on appeal, however, executive authority over visa policy could be interpreted more broadly.

The case could eventually reach the Supreme Court if lower courts issue conflicting decisions or if the legal questions are considered sufficiently important.

The Supreme Court’s approach would be closely watched because it has previously recognised significant presidential authority over immigration and entry restrictions, while also requiring executive actions to be grounded in statutory authority.

The outcome would therefore depend heavily on how the policy is legally characterised: as an exercise of delegated executive discretion or as an attempt to override the immigration scheme enacted by Congress.

Until higher courts intervene, the district court’s ruling represents an important legal defeat for the administration and strengthens the position of applicants challenging the suspension.

The State Department had not immediately commented on the decision, leaving the administration’s formal litigation strategy uncertain.

What could this ruling mean for legal immigration to the United States?

The immediate impact is potentially significant for immigrant visa applicants from the 75 affected countries because the ruling removes a major categorical obstacle to their applications.

If the decision remains in force and is implemented without a stay, consular officers may once again need to adjudicate eligible applications individually rather than applying the blanket nationality-based suspension.

That does not mean every affected applicant will receive a visa. Applicants still must satisfy all normal legal requirements, including eligibility standards, documentation rules, admissibility checks and any applicable public-charge assessment.

The practical difference is that nationality alone should no longer prevent the application from being considered under the legal framework described by the court.

For families, this could be particularly consequential. U.S. citizens and lawful residents sponsoring relatives from affected countries may see long-delayed cases resume, although administrative backlogs could continue to slow processing.

The ruling may also affect how the administration designs future immigration restrictions. Agencies could shift toward narrower policies based on individual risk factors if courts continue rejecting broad categorical measures.

More broadly, the case highlights the central role of the judiciary in U.S. immigration policy. Presidents have substantial authority to shape enforcement priorities and entry rules, but immigration remains heavily governed by statutes enacted by Congress.

That means major executive initiatives can face judicial intervention when courts conclude that agencies have exceeded delegated powers.

The ruling also demonstrates the distinction between restricting unlawful immigration and restricting legal immigration. The applicants affected by this policy were pursuing formal visa channels established by federal law.

For the administration, this creates a politically important challenge. Policies presented as part of a broader immigration-control agenda may receive different judicial treatment when they restrict people already complying with legal application procedures.

The larger consequence may therefore be institutional rather than numerical. The case reinforces the principle that even an administration pursuing sweeping immigration reform must operate within statutory limits unless Congress changes the law itself.

I have talked to a few immigrants over the years, gardeners from Mexico, who have shared their often harrowing stories of getting here so they can work. title: 'It's all very chaotic': Inside the Bay Area's mass immigration hearings - The Mercury News
description:
The woman’s case is part of a surging docket now straining Concord’s immigration court, following the Trump administration’s firing of local immigration judges and its near-total closure this year of the Bay Area’s only other immigration court in San Francisco.
In May and June, immigration courts across the country began holding the mass hearings, according to attorneys and advocates.
The push to resolve cases comes as the agency has fired more than 100 immigration judges, including at least 14 in the Bay Area.
“The message is to judges: move forward, move faster, order people removed,” said Jeremiah Johnson, a former San Francisco immigration judge fired last year.
Even before that decision, Concord had a backlog of around 60,000 cases, according to immigration court data gathered by Syracuse University.
text:
Inside a crowded courtroom on the 10th floor of a Concord office building, a three-year-old girl in pink Minnie Mouse sneakers climbed into her mother’s lap as the Mexican mother of five turned to face a black-robed judge.

Moments earlier, the judge had told the woman and the two dozen other migrants in the courtroom they had been summoned because the federal government sought to deport them. At least a dozen more sat outside in the waiting area for their cases to be heard.

The judge asked the woman, accompanied by her five children, whether she wanted more time to find an attorney before scheduling her next court date. “Sí,” she replied, nodding to an interpreter.

After the hearing, the woman, whom the Bay Area News Group is not identifying to avoid influencing her case, explained in Spanish that she came to the United States in 2024 with her family to escape gang violence overwhelming their home state of Michoacán. She had feared cartel members would come for her two teenage boys, as they did for her brother, who she said disappeared six years ago.

“They took him, and they never returned him,” she said.

The woman’s case is part of a surging docket now straining Concord’s immigration court, following the Trump administration’s firing of local immigration judges and its near-total closure this year of the Bay Area’s only other immigration court in San Francisco. The Concord court is now left with just 10 judges as it has begun taking on roughly 115,000 pending cases from San Francisco.

Under pressure from federal officials to clear an immense case backlog, Concord has begun holding mass hearings with as many as 100 people, often including families with small children, according to local attorneys. Immigrants who fail to show up risk immediate deportation orders, which have soared alongside the fast-tracked proceedings.

Immigration advocates say growing numbers of migrants with credible fears of returning to their home countries are receiving removal orders after missing the hearings due to late notice from the court or because their hearing dates are suddenly rescheduled after being set years in advance, raising due process concerns. In June, the month the mass hearings began, removal orders for failing to appear at the Concord court more than doubled to 1,046, according to a recent analysis of court data by independent immigration researchers Joseph Gunther and Brandon Marrow.

“It’s all very chaotic,” said Milli Atkinson, director of the San Francisco Bar Association’s Immigrant Legal Defense Program. “They’re constantly shifting priority for which cases move forward and which cases don’t.”

Unlike criminal or civil courts, immigration courts are part of the executive branch and must follow directives under the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, including the dismissal of immigration judges nationwide and tightening restrictions on granting migrants asylum protections in the U.S.

In May and June, immigration courts across the country began holding the mass hearings, according to attorneys and advocates. While the proceedings appear to have begun without any formal announcement, the administration has recently issued guidelines to expedite immigration cases and publicly stated that clearing backlogs is a top priority.

Trump officials have blamed the Biden administration for the backlogs, totaling more than 3 million cases nationwide, accusing it of accepting millions of people seeking asylum into the U.S. without proper vetting.

“A large backlog works to the advantage of aliens without meritorious claims and encourages further illegal migration by aliens who pose a threat to life and property as described by President Trump,” the Department of Justice, which oversees immigration courts, wrote in a March memo to Congress.

The department did not respond to questions about whether it ordered the mass hearings and why, or about advocates’ due process concerns.

The push to resolve cases comes as the agency has fired more than 100 immigration judges, including at least 14 in the Bay Area. The administration has begun hiring new judges whom it says will “restore integrity” to the immigration system. But many former judges — including some who allege they were dismissed over their prior advocacy for immigrants — contend the firings are part of a broader effort to increase deportations.

“The message is to judges: move forward, move faster, order people removed,” said Jeremiah Johnson, a former San Francisco immigration judge fired last year.

In June, the administration also abruptly closed San Francisco’s main immigration court, leaving just two judges to continue hearing cases there, but under the Concord court’s jurisdiction. Federal officials said they shuttered the court, one of the busiest in the country, handling cases from across the Central Valley and Northern California, to save costs.

Even before that decision, Concord had a backlog of around 60,000 cases, according to immigration court data gathered by Syracuse University. Now, federal officials say almost all of San Francisco’s 115,000-case backlog is expected to be transferred to Concord by the end of the year.

As the Concord court takes on more cases from both San Francisco and its existing backlog, it’s left with eight judges, down from at least 30 across the two courts before the mass firings. Some judges hired to replace those fired preside remotely over courtrooms from as far as Texas, immigration attorneys said.

At a hearing this month, Judge Lauren Black appeared via video call for a morning docket of 86 cases — about three times the size of what had been a typical case-scheduling proceeding, according to Johnson. It was unclear from where Black had called in to the hearing, which was separate from the hearing that included the woman who fled from Mexico.

Black reminded immigrants cycling through the fluorescent-lit courtroom that if they missed a future court date, she may order them removed from the country, leaving them vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation. After making her way through the docket, she determined half of those summoned to court hadn’t attended the hearing.

However, the Department of Homeland Security attorney representing the administration had failed to upload all of the necessary documentation for the judge to review remotely before deciding whether to issue removal orders. It was a heavy caseload that day, the attorney explained, and she needed more time. The judge agreed to postpone the rulings until an upcoming hearing, but cautioned there was no guarantee she would be able to issue them then.

Outside the courtroom the day prior, the woman from Mexico said she was confident her case wouldn’t end in a deportation order. She said she planned to hire an immigration attorney, who is also representing a relative, to help with her case.

Even as more than 90% of the 140-plus asylum decisions judges issued in Concord this June were denied — up from 23% in the same month in 2024, before Trump took office — the woman remained undeterred, saying she would file an appeal if her claim is rejected.

Asked what she hoped for her future if allowed to remain in the country, the woman, now staying with her sister in Manteca, said her goal would be to obtain a work permit and find a steady job to support her family.

“Whatever it is, I’m not picky,” she said. “I came here to succeed.”

text:
President Donald Trump's immigration agenda suffered another legal setback on Friday after a federal judge struck down an administration policy that suspended the processing of immigrant visas for people from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia.

The ruling is the latest in a series of court defeats for the administration's immigration policies. It follows a June decision in which a federal judge blocked another Trump administration measure that made it harder for immigrants from dozens of countries to obtain asylum, work permits, green cards and citizenship benefits.

The decision marks another challenge to Trump's efforts to tighten immigration restrictions during his second term. The affected countries span Africa, Asia, Europe and the Middle East, potentially impacting thousands of people seeking to immigrate to the United States.

Read More on News

The case also raises questions about the extent of executive branch authority over visa policy and whether broad nationality-based restrictions can be imposed without explicit congressional authorization.

What Happened?

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas in New York vacated the State Department policy, ruling that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority when he ordered consular officials to stop processing immigrant visas from 75 countries whose nationals the administration deemed more likely to require public assistance in the United States.

Vargas wrote that the policy was "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority" and conflicted with the Immigration and Nationality Act. She found that Congress gave consular officers the responsibility to determine visa eligibility on an individual basis rather than through blanket restrictions tied to nationality.

According to the ruling, the policy "categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant," undermining the statutory framework established by Congress.

Countries Affected

The policy applied to nationals of 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, among others. The Trump administration had argued that immigrants from those nations were more likely to rely on public assistance programs after arriving in the United States.

Legal Challenge

The lawsuit was brought by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals affected by the restrictions. Plaintiffs included people whose relatives had been denied visas as well as foreign nationals seeking to immigrate through employment-based petitions.

Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network (CLINIC), said in a statement that the ruling may enable some families separated by the visa restrictions to continue the immigration process, saying, "We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together."

African Communities Together, another plaintiff in the case, described the decision as "a tremendous victory for the rule of law," and argued that the policy had unfairly separated families.

The State Department defended the administration's broader approach to immigration screening, saying it was focused on "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants."

The department declined to comment on the lawsuit because litigation remains ongoing.

When the policy was first implemented, the State Department cited data indicating that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from the affected countries received some form of public assistance. Officials said the measure was part of an effort to ensure prospective immigrants would not become a charge to the public.

What Happens Next?

The decision immediately invalidates the visa-processing restrictions unless a higher court intervenes. The administration could appeal the ruling, setting up another legal battle over the limits of presidential authority on immigration matters.

For now, the ruling represents the latest judicial obstacle for an administration that has repeatedly seen its immigration measures challenged in federal courts.

title: Tri-Cities families part of thousands bilked by lawyer's alleged immigration scam
description:

Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) listed Lozano’s firm as the attorney of record, according to a disciplinary notice from the Washington State Bar Association.

She also recommended that former clients update their mailing address with Citizenship and Immigration Services because Lozano’s firm used its office address to receive clients’ immigration mail.
“He told me to memorize it and send it to my children in case immigration arrests me,” she said.
text:
A 62-year-old Mexican woman who lives in Tri-Cities spent five years searching for an attorney who could help adjust her immigration status in the United States.

She said five law firms in Washington state had already told her it wasn’t possible because she had entered the country illegally several times.

Then a friend suggested she contact immigration attorney Alexandra Lozano, who branded herself as the Abogada de los Milagros or “The Lawyer of Miracles.” Lozano claimed she could secure legal status in some of the most complicated immigration cases in the country.

“Other attorneys told me I didn’t qualify for a green card because I have a deportation order. But she said it was possible,” said “Ana, who works in agriculture. She agreed to share her story on condition the Herald not use her real name.

Ana paid about $15,000 for Lozano’s legal services in 2023, never imagining that three years later the attorney who often promoted herself alongside images of La Virgen de Guadalupe, a revered religious figure among many Mexicans, would shut down her law firm amid a fraud investigation.

Today, Lozano’s whereabouts in the U.S. are unknown to federal authorities investigating her for fraud.

Ana is one of 807 immigrants in the Tri-Cities and across Central and Eastern Washington who had reported by mid-July that they had paid thousands of dollars and were left in limbo after Lozano surrendered her law license and disappeared, according to the Central Washington Legal Aid, based in Yakima.

This region accounts for 17% of Lozano’s former clients who have contacted the law firm leading the civil complaint against her, wanting their money back and other compensation.

“And it could be more because this data is just based on people that have contacted the firm,” said Eillish Villa Malone, director of Immigration Legal Services at Central Washington Legal Aid. “We know there’s a big concentration of former clients in Central Washington because she had her office in Yakima.”

Since June 10, when Lozano closed her law office, at least 100 Tri-Citians have attended legal clinics where attorneys and legal advocates have advised them on what to do now that they no longer have legal representation, said Marichuy Alvízar, executive director of Unidos Nueva Alianza, one of the organizations providing legal assistance.

Lozano’s law firm also operated out of Tukwila and had support offices in Colombia, Mexico and Argentina, according to the civil complaint.

Across the United States, more than 35,000 clients were left without a lawyer after Lozano shut down her practice.

Nearly 54,000 immigration applications filed with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) listed Lozano’s firm as the attorney of record, according to a disciplinary notice from the Washington State Bar Association.

The three-law-firm team leading the civil complaint against Lozano estimates her payment agreements with clients total more than $400 million.

The lawsuit says the attorneys reached that estimate using Lozano’s average legal fees of about $10,000 to $15,000 per client and the number of people she represented.

How the lawsuit against Lozano began

Before her suspected fraud became public, the Washington Attorney General’s Office was investigating Lozano’s firm through July 2025 to determine if it engaged in deceptive and unfair business practices, according to documents obtained by The Seattle Times.

In April 2026, the legal team leading the civil complaint, Aric S. Bomsztyk of Tomlinson Bomsztyk Rus, Omar Barraza of Barraza Law, and Metz Law Group, launched a website announcing legal action against Lozano and asking former clients who believed they had been harmed to contact them.

After that effort began, Lozano changed the name of her firm to Luz Legal.

In early May, nine former clients filed a 50-page federal lawsuit against Ally Lozano LLC and En Solidaridad, a now-dissolved company that conducted psychological evaluations for people seeking to adjust their immigration status.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, accuses Lozano of legal malpractice, breach of contract and fiduciary duty and violation of the Consumer Protection Act.

It was filed while Lozano was also under investigation by the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Shortly afterward, on May 26, Lozano gave up her law license while facing a disciplinary hearing before the Washington State Bar Association over alleged professional misconduct.

By giving up her law license, Lozano is no longer allowed to practice law in any state or remain affiliated with the law firm she founded, said Sara Niegowski, a spokesperson for the Washington State Bar Association.

In a statement published on June 10, Luz Legal, Alexandra Lozano’s law firm, said it was forced to shut down after facing what it described as unfair scrutiny in recent years.

The firm said a team of attorneys “who may have worked on your case” is available to represent former clients and it would send former clients a copy of their case files within 60 days. “Although the process may take longer,” the statement reads.

Former clients who haven’t received their files can contact Luz Legal online.

The firm also said it’s reviewing cases individually to determine whether clients are eligible for a refund.

“Please note that if your case has already been filed, you may not be entitled to a refund,” the statement reads.

Tri-Cities clients speak out

The day Ana walked into Lozano’s office, she said she only remembers asking one of the firm’s employees what services they offered and how she could pay for them.

The employee told her she could apply for lawful permanent residency through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994, or VAWA, a law that provides immigration protections for victims of domestic violence by a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident who have experienced “battery or extreme cruelty.”

Those petitions made up most of the immigration cases Lozano’s firm handled, along with T visas for victims of human trafficking, according to the lawsuit filed in May.

People applying under VAWA generally don’t have to leave the United States while their case is pending, while a T visa can provide lawful immigration status to eligible trafficking victims.

Villa Malone said some asylum seekers were also affected after Lozano’s firm closed, although they don’t make up the majority of the former clients seeking legal help.

The employee told Ana the firm would charge a $10,500 legal fee, plus five additional Citizenship and Immigration Services-related costs for immigration waivers, a psychological evaluation, a medical exam and an interpreter.

“I paid $2,500 that day and then $500 a month for 21 months. I also paid the two waivers that cost $930 each and the psychologist, which cost $1,200,” Ana said, while holding the checklist of documents she had been told to gather for her case.

“When I found out she had closed her firm, I had already gone through such a stressful time that I just thought, ‘It’s in God hands.’”

Maria, a 59-year-old Mexican woman who also lives in the Tri-Cities, said she remembers receiving the same explanation from one of Lozano’s employees when she visited the office. She also asked that her real name be withheld.

She said the employee didn’t pressure her to hire the firm, but explained the law firm had other payment options after Maria said she only had $200 her husband had given her to begin the process of legalizing her status.

Another attorney had already told Maria her case would be difficult because she had a deportation order after entering the United States multiple times. To obtain legal status, she would have to leave the country for 10 years, the attorney told her during a phone call before she contacted Lozano’s firm.

Maria came to the United States from Mexico with her mother when she was 17.

In 1998, she went to Mexico because her father died. When she tried to return to her family, she was denied entry, so she crossed the border without authorization.

She has had a deportation order ever since.

“I was pregnant with my youngest son, and they wouldn’t let me back in,” she said. “Now all of my children can go to Mexico whenever they want because they were born here. But I can’t.”

Lozano’s employee told her she could pay in installments over three years if she made a $1,500 down payment. Maria paid that amount in cash with money her son gave her.

“Then I paid $350 with my credit card every month and I think I ended up paying about $13,000,” she said. “I still had seven payments left when the office closed.”

Testimony from nearly a dozen former employees cited by The Seattle Times said Lozano pressured staff to sign up more immigrant clients.

Employees allegedly received bonuses if they convinced people to sign contracts during their first visit or reached certain quotas for new clients.

The former employees also said their primary job was explaining how clients could apply for lawful permanent residency through VAWA. According to two former employees, they followed a script that described the law as covering situations in which a spouse constantly checked a person’s phone or monitored their social media accounts.

The former employees, however, said they didn’t fabricate information provided by clients.

The Washington State Bar Association said in a statement of alleged misconduct that Lozano’s firm asked clients to sign blank documents, which were later attached to immigration filings the clients had never reviewed.

While it remains unclear what false information was included in every case, attorneys who have reviewed former clients’ files said they have found domestic violence claims that were allegedly fabricated or exaggerated, involving clients’ spouses or children.

The bar association also said the firm used clients’ signatures to submit immigration forms containing false information without first allowing them to review the documents. Some of those applications were later denied.

“It’s called (signing) with a wet signature,” said Villa Malone. “So with a pen you gotta sign it and you gotta review everything. And what the firm was doing was signing things with stamped signatures, like somehow getting digitally the signature from the person and then stamping them on.”

As part of the VAWA process, applicants must undergo a psychological evaluation documenting the effects of the abuse they experienced.

Maria said she became suspicious of the psychologist who evaluated her.

“The law firm insisted that I complete my evaluation with that specific psychologist,” she said.

The psychological evaluation was conducted by En Solidaridad, a company founded by Lozano that was run by Manuel Lozano Rodriguez, whom Lozano had married several years earlier, according to records from the Washington Secretary of State cited by the Times.

Left with unanswered questions

Neither Ana nor Maria remembers whether they signed blank documents.

Ana said she has evidence of physical abuse by her husband and believes her case could still qualify for VAWA.

Maria said the abuse she experienced was verbal.

Earlier this year, president Donald Trump directed federal agencies to strengthen fraud detection in VAWA-based immigration petitions.

Neither woman knows whether Lozano, as alleged in other cases, submitted their applications with fabricated or exaggerated accounts of abuse.

Villa Malone said it’s possible that some applications filed by Lozano’s firm accurately reflected what clients reported.

“Not all the cases submitted by that firm were fraudulent. A lot of them are getting extra scrutiny, but not all of the cases are out of luck,” she said.

She urged former clients like Ana and Maria to attend a legal clinic, where they can get help filing a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to obtain copies of every document Lozano submitted on their behalf.

“And then get a second opinion, just so they can be aware if their application is OK and ask, ‘Are there any red flags? Am I even eligible for what I applied for?’” Villa Malone suggested.

She also recommended that former clients update their mailing address with Citizenship and Immigration Services because Lozano’s firm used its office address to receive clients’ immigration mail.

Villa Malone said it’s important for former clients to find out whether they have an upcoming immigration court hearing. Missing a hearing could further damage their cases.

“Before Trump, the case would just get denied and then nothing would happen,” Villa Malone said. “But now there is a slight risk because this administration is putting denied cases into removal proceedings.”

Maria said she doesn’t know how she will pay off the debt she took on to hire Lozano. Her husband recently underwent surgery, and she has struggled to work as she continues dealing with the effects of stomach cancer diagnosed eight years ago.

Ana said a private immigration attorney told her it would cost $25,000 just to represent her at her immigration court hearing.

“I can’t afford it because it’s too much money,” she said.

Through the civil lawsuit, the three law firms leading the case are asking the court to place Lozano’s assets into a trust for the benefit of former clients who joined the lawsuit. The number of plaintiffs nearly quadrupled from May to July.

Among the assets identified in court filings is a pink-and-white Bombardier private jet valued at about $25 million, bearing the word “abogada,” which means attorney in Spanish, and the logo of a woman with long hair.

The lawsuit also identifies a multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio that includes properties in Mexico.

Maria said she doesn’t plan to join the lawsuit because Lozano also helped her obtain a work permit.

Attorneys for several former Lozano clients told the Times that receiving work permits increased their confidence in the firm and led them to recommend her to friends and relatives.

Applicants seeking lawful permanent residency are often eligible to receive temporary work authorization while their cases are pending.

Maria’s work permit expires in 2030. She said she now uses it to work in agriculture sporadically.

Michelle Carney, an immigration attorney who serves on state and national legal ethics committees, told the Times that filing a green card application for someone who doesn’t qualify can put that person at risk.

“It exposes that person to the risk of being placed into removal proceedings,” she said.

Maria said another attorney advised her to memorize her alien registration number in case she is ever detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“He told me to memorize it and send it to my children in case immigration arrests me,” she said. “With that number they can find me. I told my husband, ‘I can’t do anything if they deport me.’ My children are grown now. Thank God they can go to Mexico.”

Ana also received a work permit and is currently using it.

When she attended a legal clinic in Richland in late July, she said she wasn’t interested in joining the civil lawsuit.

“Where can I go to tell my story?” she asked two weeks later.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — Springfield residents and advocates are reacting to reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and arrests in the city over the last week, including the detention of a local pastor described by a faith group as a prominent member of the Haitian community.

The mayor of Springfield has confirmed ICE’s presence in the city. ICE has previously said that it does not comment on ongoing operations.

G92, a faith group in Springfield, said one of the people detained, Gilbert Joubert Adrien, was a local pastor and a well-known religious leader in the Haitian community.

“He’s well-known and regarded in the Haitian community,” G92 spokesperson Michael McCrelland said. “He’s a religious leader, which in any community is important, but particularly so among the Haitians. And to snatch him up like ICE has done is just a gut punch to the people who are trying to barely get by here already.”

Advocates said ICE’s presence has had a broader effect on the Haitian community. In an interview with Spectrum News earlier in August, James Pepitho Fleurijean, with the Haitian Support Center, said some people were afraid to leave their homes or open their businesses.

“As you can tell, most of the Haitian business, they are all closed,” Fleurijean said. “The restaurant, the stores, everything they shut down completely. And the people are not really coming out.”

At least one Haitian restaurant in the area was closed outside its typical hours, though the exact reason was unknown. Kevin Bonecutter said he drove from Cincinnati to support the restaurant but found it empty.

“It’s just like a dagger right into my heart,” Bonecutter said. “Just the belief of living in America, we should be free. We should be able to live in the streets and not be afraid of walking down the streets or coming to work and just running our own business and being detained.”

The developments come after Springfield drew national attention during the 2024 presidential debate. The city has remained a focus in national immigration discussions.

During a visit Friday, Republican Vice President JD Vance received applause from some attendees as he discussed deportation efforts and job growth.

“For the first time in my life, America saw net migration out of the country as we sent millions of illegal immigrants back home,” Vance said.

Vance also said he was proud of job growth among native-born Americans.

“As a result of that, this is maybe the thing I’m most proud of in the last 18 months,” Vance said. “Do you know that all net job growth over the past 18 months went to native-born Americans, reversing a trend for four years where it all went to other people?”

Ohio Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker said she disagrees with the ongoing deportation effort and supports the Haitian community remaining in Springfield.

“I welcome the Haitian community because they should feel safe there,” Knickerbocker said. “They are not safe if they go home to Haiti. And so it is important for those that are willing to contribute to our society, build businesses, pay taxes, that they get to remain here.”

It is not known how long ICE will continue operating in Springfield. Haitian immigrants lost their temporary protected status earlier this year.

text:
Afghan Voice Agency (AVA): This policy, which took effect on January 21 of this year, suspended the issuance of immigrant visas for citizens of countries including Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia, Bosnia and Albania, and a number of countries in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean. The US State Department cited the “high risk of applicants becoming a financial burden on the government” as the reason for this action.

In his ruling, Judge Vargas ruled that the Immigration and Nationality Act does not allow the Secretary of State to block visas based solely on an applicant’s nationality. He said that the assessment of each applicant’s potential financial burden must be made on an individual basis, taking into account factors such as age, family status, assets, education and skills. The judge, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, called the policy a “direct violation” of the legal framework established by Congress.

The ruling was issued in response to a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups including the Catholic Immigration Legal Network and African Communities Together, as well as a number of visa applicants and U.S. citizens who sponsored family members from countries covered by the policy.

Under the ruling, the State Department can no longer deny or block immigrant visa applications based solely on the applicant’s nationality, and cases must be reviewed on an individual basis. However, this ruling does not mean that other restrictions on entry to the United States or the immediate issuance of visas for all applicants will be lifted, and each case must still meet its legal requirements.

It is worth noting that the Trump administration has imposed extensive restrictions on immigration during its second term in office, which has faced legal backlash and criticism from human rights groups. These groups believe that some of these policies violate the legal rights of immigrants and lead to racial discrimination. The US State Department has not responded to the ruling by the time this news was published.
